source.title: Defending Our Privacy With Backdoors
source.authors: Dominik Hintersdorf; Lukas Struppek; D. Neider; K. Kersting

record.file_problem: not stated; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper evaluates a backdoor-based privacy defense for CLIP using identity inference, not recovery of targeted knowledge in LLMs through the attacks named in the claim. Its results concern a related but different construct.
record.gate_note: The paper reports IDIA true-positive rates after its backdoor fine-tuning, but IDIA tests whether a person's data was used for training; it does not recover targeted knowledge. The paper does not test fine-tuning recovery, activation-direction ablation, quantization, or prompt-only recovery. Rows are recorded as related findings and linked to no claim version.
record.test_reason: The paper proposes a backdoor-based unlearning defense for CLIP text and image encoders. It reports only its own method's success, measured by identity inference TPR and utility. No version is tested. The system is a vision-language encoder, not an LLM. No post-unlearning recovery attack is run: no relearning, no direction ablation, no quantization, and no prompt or synonym attack. The paper does not test or use the shallow-unlearning finding as a premise. Its link to the claim is limited to discussing unlearning in general and one untested hypothesis that synonyms could bypass text-encoder unlearning.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that backdoor remapping removes names and faces from CLIP encoders with little utility loss, defeating IDIA. Text encoders reach zero TPR. Image encoders are harder, with rising residual TPR as more identities are removed. Defending both encoders gives zero TPR at all tested counts.
record.recipe_differences: A newly proposed backdoor-remapping defense for CLIP text and image encoders; it is not one of the claim's LLM unlearning recipes.
record.method_sensitivity: For image encoders, IDIA TPR rises as more identities are removed and differs by architecture; weight regularization generally preserves utility but can weaken defense success. Text-encoder IDIA TPR is reported as zero across tested name counts and regularization settings.

fits_no_version.finding: Backdoor remapping cuts identity-inference TPR from 100% to 0% for text encoders at all name counts. Image encoders keep residual TPR that grows with the number of identities removed (up to ~50% for ResNet-50). Weight regularization trades defense success for utility.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Backdoor-based embedding remapping removes name–face associations from CLIP against IDIA. Effectiveness depends on modality, architecture and removal scale.

record.problems: The outcome is IDIA privacy inference, not knowledge recovery or targeted-knowledge accuracy. The paper evaluates one proposed defense family on CLIP rather than the listed LLM unlearning methods. Some combined-encoder outcomes are available only in figures.
record.rows_left_out: Within the 60-row limit, omitted most ViT-L/14 text-encoder name-count rows, the combined text-and-image encoder's other removal-count rows, and utility/performance metrics such as ImageNet accuracy, similarity scores, and other dataset results. The reported ViT-L/14 text results are described as identical to ViT-B/32; see Tables 2, 5–6 and Figures 2–3, 7–12 and Appendix B.

untested.parts: Whether an LLM unlearning method holds up under simple recovery attacks. The study covers a CLIP encoder only and runs no recovery attack.
Relearning or fine-tuning after unlearning to restore removed identities.
Activation-direction ablation, or analysis of blocking versus deletion. The remapping-to-neutral-embedding design is never probed for residual knowledge.
Rephrasing, synonym or nickname prompts, jailbreaks, other languages. Synonym bypass is only hypothesized in the Limitations section, not tested.
No claim of robustness to recovery attacks is made or tested.

record.verdict_notes: Not an LLM study. The evaluation is a single privacy attack, with no adversarial recovery attempt. The authors themselves flag possible synonym bypass ('Terminator' vs. the actor's name) as untested. After removing 64 faces, image-encoder FaceScrub zero-shot accuracy falls to 0.24% (Table 3), suggesting faces in general were damaged. This is a collateral cost but irrelevant to any version here.

versions.untested_parts: No targeted-knowledge accuracy or recovery attack is measured; IDIA is a privacy membership/identity inference attack.
No post-unlearning fine-tuning attack is tested.
No activation-direction ablation or analysis of access blocking versus deletion is tested.
No rephrasing, jailbreak, other-language, or in-context recovery attack is tested.
The paper does not test a method for resisting the attacks named in the claim.
